title: The builder returns a SuffixArray built in memory
body:
`SuffixArrayBuilder::build_to_file` writes the file and returns `()`, and every caller then opens the file with `SuffixArray::open`. With memory scratch, `construct` holds the sorted suffix array at its end as one `Memory<W>` buffer per partition, and `write` is only the concatenation into the file. There is no way to get a `SuffixArray` without a file.

## Proposal

`TypedSuffixArray::new(filename: Option<String>, header, text: T, suffixes: S, lcps: Option<S>, max_query_len, subsample)` is the one generic constructor over arrays already in hand. `open` reads a file's arrays and calls it.

`SuffixArrayBuilder::build(self) -> Result<SuffixArray>` builds with memory scratch, concatenates the partitions into one `Memory<W>` for the suffix array and one for the LCP array, applying the boundary LCPs as `write` does, and calls `new` with the text it holds. It dispatches over the width in two arms, the way `typed::open` dispatches over width and storage, and no impl block fixes a parameter. `build_to_file` is unchanged.

`lcps` becomes `Option<S>`, so a file build reads the LCP array from disk as now and an in-memory build holds it. `filename` becomes `Option<String>`; `metadata()` reports the file's name, size and modified time only when there is one, and the subsample is computed directly when there is no file to key a cache on.

## Cost

- `Metadata.filename`, `modified` and `file_size` become `Option`, and `summary()` emits their rows only when present. The CLI's `summarize` output for a file is unchanged.
- `construct` changes, so the build is benchmarked before and after.
- A test builds the same input both ways and compares suffixes, LCPs, text and a search.
